# The question {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## How good is your model, really?

You fit a model of European productivity growth. It explains 78% of the variance.

Three different questions hide inside "how good is it?":

::: {.tight}
- How well does it fit **the data you used**? (Almost meaningless.)
- How well would it do on **a new country**?
- How well would it do **next year**?
:::

::: {.warn}
Those last two are different questions, and they need **different splits**. Get
the split wrong and every number that follows is optimistic.
:::

## The decomposition

For squared loss, at a point $x_0$:

$$\mathbb{E}\big[(y_0 - \hat{f}(x_0))^2\big] = \underbrace{\operatorname{Bias}^2(\hat f)}_{\text{too rigid}} + \underbrace{\operatorname{Var}(\hat f)}_{\text{too sensitive}} + \underbrace{\sigma^2}_{\text{irreducible}}$$

::: {.tight}
- **Bias** falls as the model gets more flexible
- **Variance** rises as the model gets more flexible
- $\sigma^2$ does not move. It is what the predictors do not observe.
:::

::: {.check}
$\sigma^2$ is not a defect of your method. Reporting a validation error below it
means you have leaked, not learned.
:::

# The trap {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## Why random K-fold breaks here

`core.parquet` is 30 countries observed over 15 years.

Random K-fold puts **Germany 2019 in training and Germany 2020 in test**.

::: {.tight}
- Countries are highly persistent — productivity this year nearly determines next year
- The model can effectively memorise the country, then "predict" it
- Your validation error measures **interpolation within a country**, not forecasting
:::

::: {.warn}
This is not a subtle statistical nicety. On this panel it is the difference
between a model that looks excellent and one that is useful.
:::

## Three splits, three questions

| Split | Answers | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **Random K-fold** | "New row from the same countries and years" | Almost never here |
| **GroupKFold by `geo`** | "A country I have never seen" | Transfer across countries |
| **TimeSeriesSplit** by `time` | "Next year" | Forecasting — Session 11 |

::: {.check}
Choose the split that matches the sentence you intend to write in your
conclusion. Then say which you used.
:::

# Doing it {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## The data

```python
import pandas as pd

core = pd.read_parquet("data/spine/core.parquet")
d = core.dropna(subset=["prod_growth"]).copy()

print(d.shape)                    # ~420 rows (first year per country has no growth)
print(d.geo.nunique(), d.time.min(), d.time.max())   # 30 countries, 2010-2024
```

::: {.muted}
`prod_growth` is NaN in each country's first year. That is arithmetic, not
missing data — you cannot difference what has no predecessor.
:::

## Set up the comparison

```python
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.model_selection import (cross_val_score, KFold,
                                     GroupKFold, TimeSeriesSplit)

X = d[["gdp_pc_eur", "population", "employment_ths", "gfcf_meur"]].fillna(0)
y = d["prod_growth"]
m = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=300, random_state=60033)

RMSE = "neg_root_mean_squared_error"
```

## Three schemes, three answers

```python
rand  = cross_val_score(m, X, y, scoring=RMSE,
                        cv=KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=60033))

group = cross_val_score(m, X, y, scoring=RMSE,
                        cv=GroupKFold(5), groups=d["geo"])

d_s = d.sort_values("time")
time_ = cross_val_score(m, X.loc[d_s.index], y.loc[d_s.index],
                        scoring=RMSE, cv=TimeSeriesSplit(5))

for n, s in [("random", rand), ("by country", group), ("by time", time_)]:
    print(f"{n:12s} RMSE {-s.mean():.3f}")
```

## What you should see

::: {.check}
Random K-fold reports the **best** error. It is also the only one answering a
question nobody asked.
:::

The gap between random and grouped is a **direct measure of how much your model
is leaning on country identity** rather than on the economics.

::: {.muted}
If grouped error is far worse, your model has learned "this is Germany", not
"this is what raises productivity".
:::

## Flexibility, drawn

```python
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor

rows = []
for depth in range(1, 16):
    t = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=depth, random_state=60033)
    cv = -cross_val_score(t, X, y, cv=GroupKFold(5), groups=d["geo"],
                          scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error").mean()
    t.fit(X, y)
    train = np.sqrt(((y - t.predict(X)) ** 2).mean())
    rows.append((depth, train, cv))
```

Plot both curves against depth.

::: {.check}
Training error falls monotonically. Validation error falls, then turns. The turn
is the bias–variance tradeoff, and it is the only one of the two curves that
tells you anything.
:::

## Leakage, the practical form

```python
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

#  WRONG — the scaler has already seen the test fold
X_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)
cross_val_score(m, X_scaled, y, cv=GroupKFold(5), groups=d["geo"])

#  RIGHT — every preprocessing step re-fits inside each fold
pipe = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), m)
cross_val_score(pipe, X, y, cv=GroupKFold(5), groups=d["geo"])
```

::: {.warn}
Any step that **learns from the data** — scaling, imputation, feature
selection, target encoding — must live inside the pipeline. This is the single
most common error in applied machine learning, and it always flatters you.
:::

## What to report

::: {.tight}
- **Which split** you used, and the sentence it licenses
- Validation error in the **units of the outcome**, not just $R^2$
- The gap between training and validation error
- The gap between random and grouped CV — your leakage diagnostic
:::

::: {.warn}
Never report a number computed on data the model was fit on. If you tuned on
it, it is training data, whatever you called the variable.
:::

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Consequence |
|---|---|
| Random K-fold on a panel | Optimistic by a wide margin |
| Scaling before splitting | Leakage; error understated |
| Tuning on the test set | The test set is now training data |
| Reporting $R^2$ only | No sense of magnitude |
| One split, one number | No sense of variability |
